title: Ethnic, religious, and occupational disparities in the prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress among Ghanaian Nurses
content:
by Grace Arthur, Reginald Quansah, Prudence Tettey

Background

Mental health disorders constitute a significant component of the disease burden among nurses, given the demanding and stressful nature of the profession. This study assessed the prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress among nurses and examined socio-cultural, demographic, lifestyle, and occupational factors associated with these conditions.

Method

A cross-sectional study involving 302 nurses was conducted at LEKMA Hospital. Socio-demographic information was collected using a structured questionnaire, and depression, anxiety, and stress were measured using the 21-item Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21), with standard scoring and severity classification. Logistic regression analysis was employed to identify ethnic, religious, and occupational factors associated with these mental health disorders.

Results

The prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress was 54.30%, 64.57%, and 37.75%, respectively. Regarding socio-cultural factors, nurses of Ewe (AOR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.22–0.75) and Ga-Dangme (AOR = 0.34; 95% CI: 0.15–0.81) ethnicity had lower odds of anxiety and stress, respectively, compared to those of Akan ethnicity; no significant associations were observed between socio-cultural factors and depression. Additionally, Traditional religious affiliation was associated with higher odds of stress compared with Christianity (AOR = 11.73; 95% CI 2.03–67.80). Among demographic factors, nurses aged 31–40 years had higher odds of anxiety than those aged ≤30 years (AOR = 1.95; 95% CI 1.05–3.63). Among lifestyle factors, physical activity was associated with lower odds of anxiety (AOR = 0.44; 95% CI 0.24–0.79) and stress (AOR = 0.44; 95% CI 0.25–0.77). In terms of occupational factors, nurses working in the in-patient department (AOR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.19–0.88) had lower odds of depression. Conversely, working night shifts, having greater work experience, and having contact with confirmed COVID-19 patients were associated with higher odds of depression. Regarding anxiety, greater work experience, and contact with confirmed COVID-19 patients were associated with higher odds of anxiety. Furthermore, working in the in-patient department (AOR = 0.27; 95% CI: 0.12–0.60) and working day shifts (AOR = 0.45; 95% CI: 0.25–0.81) were associated with lower odds of stress. In contrast, working night shifts, having greater work experience, and working longer hours were associated with higher odds of stress.

Conclusion

This investigation revealed a high prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress among nurses at LEKMA Hospital and identified key socio-cultural, demographic, lifestyle, and occupational factors. These findings underscore an urgent need for interventions that are sensitive to religious and ethnic diversity. Furthermore, workplace promotion and support programs should target occupational stressors to enhance overall nursing well-being.
author: Grace Arthur
